title: alertrouter · LGTM
description: Alert flow and routing decisions, Sigil evaluation throughput and latency, k6 load measurements and policy reloads, across Mimir metrics, Tempo traces, Loki logs and Pyroscope profiles. Team filters the alert, evaluation and policy panels; Load run filters the k6 panels. Profiles cover the whole process.

panels.title: Service up
panels.description: The latest Alloy scrape of alertrouter, stored in Mimir. DOWN means the scrape failed; no data means the pipeline has not delivered a sample.

panels.title: Firing alerts routed
panels.description: Firing alerts that ended in a notification in the selected time range and team, whatever the outcome: routed by the team's policy, or sent to the default because the alert had no known team, an invalid severity, or its evaluation failed. Resolved alerts are acknowledged, not routed, and don't count.

panels.title: Failed reloads
panels.description: Team bundle loads the compiler rejected in the selected time range. Each one left the previous bundle serving.

panels.title: Reload health
panels.description: Whether the latest load of the team bundle succeeded, from alertrouter_policy_last_reload_successful. FAILING means the latest attempt was rejected and the previous bundle keeps serving, on any replica: the stat takes the lowest value; it stays FAILING until a load succeeds, however long nobody touches the bundle. Alert on this: alertrouter_policy_last_reload_successful == 0 for 5m.

panels.title: Last successful reload
panels.description: Seconds since the team bundle last loaded successfully, on the replica that loaded it longest ago. Reloads only happen when the policies directory changes, on SIGHUP or on request, so a large value is normal for a bundle nobody edits: an idle week and a week of rejected edits look the same here. Read it next to Reload health, which tells the two apart.

panels.title: Pages
panels.description: Pages dispatched in the selected time range: critical production alerts, and warnings that kept firing past the team's page_after. Counted at the notifier, so every team, including pages a failed evaluation fell back to; Team doesn't filter it.

panels.title: Drops
panels.description: Alerts dropped in the selected time range: muted by the team, or not from production. A drop is still logged and counted, so a dropped alert is never lost without a trace. Counted at the notifier; Team doesn't filter it.

panels.title: Channel notifications
panels.description: Alerts posted to a channel in the selected time range: routine warnings to the team channel, a team's own routing, and everything no rule matched to #alerts. Counted at the notifier; Team doesn't filter it.

panels.title: Routed by fallback
panels.description: Firing alerts in the selected time range the team's policy didn't decide: unowned (no team label, or a team the directory doesn't know), invalid (a severity the kind doesn't have) or failed (the evaluation errored or timed out). Each still went out, as the kind's default or the fallback decision, but someone should fix the alert rule or the policy. Unowned alerts carry the team -, which only All selects. Zero is the goal.

panels.title: Alerts received by status
panels.description: Alerts per second in the webhook batches Alertmanager posts, firing and resolved. Resolved alerts are acknowledged and not routed. Single alerts posted to /api/v1/teams/:team/route don't come through a webhook and don't count here.

panels.title: Firing alerts by outcome
panels.description: Firing alerts per second, stacked by how they were routed: routed by the team's policy, unowned, invalid or failed. Every firing alert lands in exactly one outcome and ends in a notification, so this is the service's whole output rate. Unowned alerts count under the team -, which only All selects.

panels.title: Notifications by destination
panels.description: Notifications dispatched per second, by decision and destination: the on-call target a page went to, or the channel a notification was posted to. A drop has no destination and shows as drop -. The demo notifier logs and counts; it doesn't call a pager or a chat service.

panels.title: Webhook batch size
panels.description: Alerts per webhook request, firing and resolved together, estimated from the histogram buckets. Alertmanager groups alerts by its route's group_by, so a large batch is usually one incident firing many alerts at once.

panels.title: Evaluations / second
panels.description: Observed rate of completed p.Eval calls, one per routed alert, over the rate window. Includes failed and timed-out evaluations. Unowned and invalid alerts go to the default without an evaluation and don't count. Follows Team, independently of Load run. This is achieved throughput at the current offered load.

panels.title: Evaluations in selected range
panels.description: Completed p.Eval calls in the selected time range and team, including failed ones.

panels.title: Mean evaluation
panels.description: Mean elapsed time around p.Eval over the selected time range. Computed from histogram sum divided by count, weighted across the selected teams. Webhook decoding, the team lookup, dispatch, response formatting and logging happen outside this timer. No evaluations means no latency value.

panels.title: Evaluations within 100 µs
panels.description: Fraction of completed p.Eval calls in the selected time range taking at most 100 microseconds, using the exact 0.0001-second histogram bucket. This is an observed latency distribution, not an SLO.

panels.title: Evaluation throughput by team
panels.description: Completed p.Eval calls per second for each team's policy, including failed evaluations. A webhook batch evaluates each firing alert on its own, against the policy of the team its team label names.

panels.title: Evaluation latency
panels.description: Elapsed time around p.Eval for the selected teams. Quantiles are estimated from the histogram buckets, whose lowest boundary is 50 microseconds. Use the mean above for the sum/count measurement. Excludes HTTP handling, policy loading, dispatch and response formatting.

panels.title: k6 · request rate
panels.description: Achieved HTTP request rate per run, route, webhook and reload requests together. Compare with the configured arrival rate; dropped iterations below expose generator saturation.

panels.title: k6 · incorrect routing
panels.description: Fraction of checked alerts whose decision, reason, target or channel didn't match the expected outcome, cumulative within each run and scenario. The expectation comes from requests/cases.json for the named cases and from the same rules as the policies for generated alerts. The suite's threshold is 0.1%; zero is the goal.

panels.title: k6 · HTTP p95 by request
panels.description: Cumulative p95 for each request type within its run: a single-alert route, a webhook batch of up to 100 alerts, or a policy reload. Values are exported in seconds. These are separate percentiles, not a combined percentile; use the JSON report for the full-run p95. Only expected responses are included here; transport and correctness failures remain visible in the incorrect-routing panel.

panels.title: k6 · HTTP p99 by request
panels.description: Cumulative p99 for each request type within its run, in seconds. A reload recompiles every team's policy while routing continues, so its latency is the compiler's, not the router's.

panels.title: k6 · alerts routed by decision
panels.description: Alerts per second k6 saw routed, by the decision alertrouter answered, from route and webhook requests together. Compare with Notifications by destination above: every firing alert k6 sends should show up on both.

panels.title: k6 · reloads under load
panels.description: Policy reloads per second the reload scenario requested while routing traffic ran, by status. Each one recompiles every team's policy and swaps it in; routing keeps answering from the last good bundle throughout, which the incorrect-routing panel confirms.

panels.title: k6 · dropped iterations
panels.description: Reported cumulative dropped iterations observed within the selected time range. k6 only emits this counter when it drops work, so retain the last observed count. Zero is shown only for runs with iteration samples. Check the JSON report for the completed run total. Breakpoint runs drop iterations by design once alertrouter saturates.

targets.expr: sum by (testid) (max_over_time(k6_dropped_iterations_total{testid=~"${load_run:regex}"}[$__range])) or on (testid) (0 * sum by (testid) (max_over_time(k6_iterations_total{testid=~"${load_run:regex}"}[$__range])))

panels.title: k6 · active virtual users
panels.description: Active virtual users reported by k6. Increase MAX_VUS only when the generator needs more concurrency, and check the load generator resources too.

panels.title: Decisions by outcome
panels.description: Decisions per second the teams' policies made, stacked by decision and reason. Only evaluated alerts count: notify unrouted here is an alert no rule matched. Unowned and invalid alerts skip the policy, and a failed evaluation made no decision; all three count under Firing alerts by outcome instead.

panels.title: Evaluation errors
panels.description: Failed evaluations per second by team and kind. conflict is two rules that decided the same reason with different payloads, such as a team page rule tying with the platform's; runtime a policy that doesn't guard against its input; assertion a failed assert; timeout an evaluation that ran past the per-alert evaluation timeout. Each failed alert still went out as the fallback decision. An empty chart means no evaluation errors in this range.

panels.title: HTTP requests by status
panels.description: API requests per second by route and status code, from the gin middleware. Only routes under /api/v1 count: the compose healthcheck polls /readyz every 5 seconds. A webhook answers 200 once every alert in it is processed, whatever each alert's outcome, because Alertmanager retries anything else; 400 is a malformed or invalid webhook, 413 a body over 1 MiB and 503 a request before the policies loaded. A single-alert route answers 404 for an unknown team, 422 for an invalid alert and 503 with the fallback decision when its evaluation failed.

panels.title: HTTP latency by route
panels.description: p95 time to answer an API request, by route, estimated from the histogram buckets. A webhook's latency grows with its batch size: it evaluates and dispatches every firing alert before it answers.

panels.title: Loaded policies
panels.description: Every team policy that serves: the team, its root policy, the fingerprint of the bundle it was compiled from, and where that bundle came from (embedded, or a mounted directory). Not filtered by team.

panels.title: Policy reloads
panels.description: Team bundle loads per interval by result: startup, the poller noticing a changed directory, SIGHUP and POST /api/v1/policies/reload. Polling only reloads when the directory changed, so an idle stack shows nothing here after startup; a load test's reload scenario shows up as a steady success rate.

panels.title: Routing traces · Tempo
panels.description: Traces with an alertrouter.route span, one per firing alert, for the selected team. Open a trace to see the alert, the decision, its reason and the candidates Sigil weighed, then use its Logs link to open the alert's log line in Loki.

panels.title: Routing logs · Loki
panels.description: One line per firing alert: the team, the decision, its reason and where it went. Expand a line and follow View trace. Explore logs includes HTTP access logs and errors too.

panels.title: CPU profile · Pyroscope
panels.description: Whole-process CPU profile over the dashboard time range, including Sigil, HTTP handling and telemetry. Click a stack frame to focus it. Profiles upload every 15 seconds. Goroutine-leak capture also runs GC, and that cost is included.

panels.title: Runtime profile · Pyroscope
panels.description: Choose Runtime profile to inspect allocations, live heap, goroutines, mutex contention, blocking or detected goroutine leaks. Types appear after samples reach Pyroscope. Whole-process data over the selected time range; empty leak data is expected in a healthy process. Heap profiles are merged over the range; the RSS chart shows process memory.

panels.title: Observability targets · Alloy scrape health
panels.description: One means Alloy can scrape the target. This complements the Compose readiness checks; it does not assert end-to-end ingestion.

panels.title: alertrouter · CPU and resident memory
panels.description: CPU is CPU-seconds per wall-clock second (cores). Memory is process RSS, not heap-only. These include telemetry overhead.
